lead: Cold below about −40 °C destroys living tissue. A cryoprobe, a metal tip cooled by liquid nitrogen or by an expanding gas, is pressed on or pushed into a lesion, and the ice that forms kills the cells. Surgeons use it on warts and skin lesions, on small kidney and liver tumours, and inside the heart to stop atrial fibrillation. The same cold, applied more gently with a protective chemical, preserves blood, semen and tissue for years inside a dewar. This chapter covers the physics, the probe, the freeze–thaw cycle and the safety rules.
prereq: You need sensible heat (Q = mcΔT), latent heat (Q = mL) and specific heat capacity from basic heat transfer; compare with diathermy, which adds heat instead of removing it.

blocks.text: Ice does not form inside the cell first. It forms in the fluid between cells. Pure water joins the ice, and the fluid left behind becomes a concentrated salt solution. The cell loses water, shrinks, and its proteins are damaged. If cooling is fast, ice also forms inside the cell, and those sharp crystals cut the membranes and organelles.

Thaw is the second half of the kill. Ice melts, water rushes back into the shrunken cell, and a membrane already weakened by the first freeze breaks. A slow thaw builds bigger crystals and does more damage than a fast thaw.
Q = m c ΔT₁ + m<sub>w</sub> L + m c<sub>f</sub> ΔT₂
blocks.where: Q is the heat removed, in joules (J); m is the mass of tissue, in kg; c is the specific heat of unfrozen tissue, about 3.5 kJ/kg·K; ΔT₁ is the fall from body temperature to freezing, in K; m<sub>w</sub> is the mass of water that freezes, in kg; L is the latent heat of fusion of water, 334 kJ/kg; c<sub>f</sub> is the specific heat of frozen tissue, about 1.8 kJ/kg·K; ΔT₂ is the fall below freezing, in K. Tissue freezes near 0 °C (in fact a degree or two below), and not all of its water freezes, so the latent term is an upper estimate.

blocks.text: A single freeze is unreliable. Surgeons therefore use the freeze–thaw–freeze cycle.

items: Freeze until the ice ball reaches a few millimetres beyond the edge of the lesion: the edge of the ice is near 0 °C, and the lethal −40 °C line lies a few millimetres inside it.
Hold for a few minutes so the cold soaks in.
Let it thaw slowly. Do not assist the thaw.
Freeze a second time, then let it thaw finally.

blocks.text: Below about −40 °C almost no cell survives. Above that temperature some cells recover and the lesion regrows. That −40 °C line inside the tissue, not the tip temperature, is the real target.

There are two ways to make a cold tip. One is to pump a cryogen, a very cold liquid, through a chamber at the tip. The other is to let a compressed gas expand through a small nozzle. Both pull heat out of the tissue by conduction.

Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C at one atmosphere. In a closed probe it flows into a small chamber at the metal tip, boils there, and the vapour leaves through the handle. The probe does not store cold, it only carries it, so the flow must be steady.

The Joule–Thomson effect is the cooling that happens when a compressed gas is forced through a narrow orifice and expands. No moving parts and no separate refrigerator are needed. A gas cools this way only below its inversion temperature; argon and nitrous oxide are below theirs at room temperature, whereas helium warms on expansion.
A thermocouple at the tip measures temperature. A small heater wire lets the surgeon warm the tip on demand, so it releases from the tissue without tearing it. That is called an active thaw.
Skin. Warts, verrucae, actinic keratosis and small skin cancers are frozen with a spray or a cotton swab for 10–30 s, twice, with a thaw between. The blister that forms lifts the dead tissue off.

Tumours. In cryoablation one or more probes are pushed into a kidney, liver, prostate or lung tumour under ultrasound or CT guidance. The ice ball is visible on the image. Two cycles are used, and the ice must cover the tumour plus a margin.
Heart. A cryoballoon freezes the tissue around the pulmonary veins, where atrial fibrillation often starts. defibrillator protection and cardiac ablation compares this with radio-frequency ablation.

Storage. Semen, embryos, stem cells, skin and rare blood units are kept frozen for years; ordinary donated red cells are not frozen but kept at about 4 °C for up to about six weeks. A cryoprotectant such as glycerol or DMSO is added first, so water leaves the cells before freezing. The sample is cooled slowly, about 1 °C per minute, and stored in a dewar, a vacuum flask, either in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C or in its vapour at about −150 °C. Thawing is fast, in a 37 °C water bath.
Liquid nitrogen is safe to use only when the cold, the gas and the pressure it makes are all controlled.

items: Cold burns and frostbite: never touch an uninsulated probe; wear a face shield and loose gloves.
Asphyxiation: one litre of liquid nitrogen gives about 700 litres of gas at room temperature, which pushes oxygen out of a closed room without any smell.
Vent the boil-off: use dewars in a ventilated space with an oxygen monitor; never seal a dewar.
Pressure: fit relief valves on any vessel that can be closed, because trapped liquid expands about 700 times when it warms.

examples.question: During cryosurgery a 1 g piece of tissue must be cooled from 37 °C to −40 °C, the lethal temperature. The tissue is 80 % water by mass and freezes at about 0 °C. Take the specific heat of tissue as 3.5 kJ/kg·K above freezing and 1.8 kJ/kg·K when frozen, and the latent heat of fusion of water as 334 kJ/kg. (a) Find the total heat removed. (b) Find the minimum mass of liquid nitrogen needed, if each kilogram of nitrogen absorbs 199 kJ as it evaporates.
steps: Convert the mass: m = 1 g = 0.001 kg.
Cooling to freezing: Q₁ = m c ΔT₁ = 0.001 kg × 3500 J/kg·K × 37 K = 129.5 J.
Freezing the water: m<sub>w</sub> = 0.8 × 0.001 kg = 0.0008 kg, so Q₂ = m<sub>w</sub> L = 0.0008 kg × 334 000 J/kg = 267.2 J.
Cooling the frozen tissue from 0 °C to −40 °C: Q₃ = m c<sub>f</sub> ΔT₂ = 0.001 kg × 1800 J/kg·K × 40 K = 72 J.
Total heat: Q = 129.5 + 267.2 + 72 = 468.7 J. The latent term is the largest; it is an upper estimate, because some water stays unfrozen.
Nitrogen needed: 468.7 J ÷ 199 000 J/kg = 2.355 × 10⁻³ kg = 2.36 g.
This is the ideal minimum. A real probe also cools the handle, the lines and the tissue around the lesion, so several times as much nitrogen is used.
examples.answer: The heat removed is 468.7 J for one gram of tissue, and the minimum liquid nitrogen needed is 2.36 g if no cold is wasted.

traps: Cryotherapy removes heat; diathermy adds heat. They are opposite treatments with similar-sounding names.
A −196 °C tip does not mean −196 °C in the tissue. The ice front must pass −40 °C at the far edge of the lesion, so probe placement and imaging decide success.
One long freeze is weaker than two shorter freezes with a slow thaw between them. A quick thaw with no second freeze under-kills and the lesion returns.
Unit slips: latent heat is 334 kJ/kg = 334 000 J/kg, not 334 J/kg, and specific heat is per kg, not per gram. A stray factor of 1000 is the commonest arithmetic error here.
Oxygen deficiency has no warning smell. Nitrogen gas is colourless and odourless, so a leaking dewar in a small room causes dizziness and collapse before anyone notices.

quiz.q: At what temperature does liquid nitrogen boil at atmospheric pressure?
Why does a slow thaw increase cell death compared with a fast thaw?
quiz.a: During a slow thaw, small ice crystals grow into larger ones (recrystallisation), and water re-enters the already damaged cell slowly, so the membrane swells and bursts. A fast thaw melts the ice before the crystals can grow.

quiz.q: State the Joule–Thomson effect and name two gases used in cryoprobes that rely on it.
quiz.a: A compressed gas forced through a narrow orifice expands and cools. Argon (about −186 °C at the tip) and nitrous oxide (about −89 °C) are used.

quiz.q: A 2.5 g lesion is frozen from 37 °C to −40 °C. It is 80 % water. Take c = 3.5 kJ/kg·K above freezing, 1.8 kJ/kg·K when frozen, and L = 334 kJ/kg. Find the heat removed.
A dewar spills 2 litres of liquid nitrogen into a closed room. Roughly how much gas is released at room temperature?
quiz.a: About 700 litres of gas per litre of liquid, so 2 × 700 = 1400 litres of nitrogen gas, enough to displace the oxygen in a small room.

quiz.q: Why is argon preferred over nitrous oxide for deep tumour cryoablation?
quiz.a: Argon reaches about −186 °C at the tip against about −89 °C for nitrous oxide. The colder tip gives a faster freeze, a larger ice ball and a −40 °C front further from the probe, so the whole tumour plus margin can be killed in two cycles.

quiz.q: A hospital keeps its liquid nitrogen dewars in an unventilated basement room. State two risks and two corrections.
quiz.a: Risks: asphyxiation from odorless nitrogen boil-off, and cold burns or pressure burst if a dewar is sealed. Corrections: move storage to a ventilated space with an oxygen monitor and alarm, and fit relief valves and keep vessels open to vent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Vitrification pushes cryopreservation further: with a high cryoprotectant concentration and very fast cooling, water becomes a glass with no ice crystals, which is how many oocytes and embryos are now banked. Argon cryoablation under MRI guidance lets the ice ball be watched in three dimensions. Good search terms: cryoablation, vitrification, Joule–Thomson cryoprobe, oxygen deficiency monitor.
